claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayers under sustained loading is governed by heterogeneous slip-system activation.
Localized lattice distortions and modified short-range order induce heterogeneous slip-system activation.
Minor additions of a larger-radius element can introduce localized lattice distortion and strain fields.
Low-dose post-deposition ion irradiation can generate controlled localized strain fields while preserving the multilayer architecture.
The induced distortions create enhanced local stress fields.
Enhanced local stress fields promote earlier dislocation nucleation.
Enhanced local stress fields produce non-uniform plastic flow compared with conventional multilayers.
Temperatures of 350–500 °C permit activation of nontraditional slip systems without full recovery.
Localized lattice distortions and altered short-range order occur in both bulk and interfacial regions of the modified multilayers.
Localized lattice distortion and altered short-range order mediate dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Local chemical order and severe localized distortion can pin dislocations, promote cross-slip, and change the plastic-deformation mechanism.
Dislocations nucleate and propagate non-uniformly across the multilayer structure because of heterogeneous slip activation.
Non-uniform dislocation nucleation and propagation cause progressive plastic deformation during sustained loading.
Modified samples should exhibit greater localized creep strain than the unmodified, unirradiated baseline.
Modified samples should exhibit an earlier onset of plasticity than the baseline.
Modified samples should exhibit a higher creep strain rate than the baseline when increased distortion correlates with earlier and more heterogeneous dislocation nucleation.
Larger interfacial lattice misfit can produce denser dislocation networks and stronger interfacial stress fields.
Stronger interfacial stress fields from lattice misfit can impede dislocation penetration and improve creep resistance.
The hypothesis applies only while nanoscale multilayer integrity is retained and catastrophic damage or unwanted phase changes are avoided.
